name: SAPS II
seoDesc: SAPS II: work out chronic diseases from the age and the heart rate. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The SAPS II calculator turns the age, the heart rate and more into chronic diseases. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the SAPS II calculator work?
sections.html:
The SAPS II calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports chronic diseases in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the BUN or serum urea and the type of admission); then you type in the age, the heart rate, the systolic blood pressure and the temperature.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the SAPS II calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Chronic diseases=-type of admission + total score − (age, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, temperature, glasgow Coma Score, urine, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, bilirubin, white blood count) − (paO₂, fiO₂) − (BUN or serum urea, BUN)
Total score=type of admission + chronic diseases + (age, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, temperature, glasgow Coma Score, urine, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, bilirubin, white blood count) + (BUN or serum urea, BUN)
Logit pb=(737 ÷ 10000) × total score + (9971 ÷ 10000) × the natural log of (total score) − 77631 ÷ 10000
Estimated mortality=(100 × the exponential of ((737 ÷ 10000) × total score + (9971 ÷ 10000) × the natural log of (total score) − 77631 ÷ 10000) ÷ (the exponential of ((737 ÷ 10000) × total score + (9971 ÷ 10000) × the natural log of (total score) − 77631 ÷ 10000) + 1))
Chronic diseases=-type of admission + total score − (age, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, temperature, glasgow Coma Score, urine, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, bilirubin, white blood count) − (paO₂, fiO₂) − (BUN or serum urea, serum urea)
Chronic diseases=-type of admission + total score − (age, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, temperature, glasgow Coma Score, urine, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, bilirubin, white blood count) − (BUN or serum urea, serum urea)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take BUN or serum urea set to BUN, Chronic diseases set to None, Type of admission set to Scheduled surgical and Total score = 10. The calculator returns Estimated mortality = 0.8748.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Estimated mortality = 0.8748 should be roughly the size you expected from BUN or serum urea set to BUN and Chronic diseases set to None.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Time, opening in days

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The SAPS II calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the age, the heart rate and the systolic blood pressure — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the SAPS II calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns chronic diseases, derived from the age, the heart rate and the systolic blood pressure. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the SAPS II calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the heart rate, the systolic blood pressure and the temperature, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Estimated mortality = 0.8748. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the SAPS II calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
